steps.text: We start with a comment reminding us this is our detection log. Then dist holds twenty distance measurements in meters, spread across two lines just so the list fits nicely.
Right below it, conf holds twenty confidence scores, one for each distance. These two lists line up position by position, so the first distance pairs with the first confidence.
This banner comment marks our histogram section. We print a title telling the reader that each hash mark stands for one detection.
We loop over lo, the low edge of each bucket, going zero, ten, twenty, up to fifty. So we're carving distances into ten-meter bands.
For each band, we count how many distances fall between lo and lo plus ten. Each true comparison counts as one, and summing them gives us n, the bucket total.
Then we print the range label, nicely padded, followed by n hash marks. Multiplying the hash string by n draws a little bar you can read at a glance.
Now the scatter section. We print a heading, starting with a newline for spacing, explaining that distance from zero to sixty meters gets squeezed into thirty columns.
We set ROWS to eight and COLS to thirty. This defines the size of our text canvas, eight rows tall and thirty columns wide.
Here we build the grid: a list of eight rows, each row a list of thirty spaces. This is our blank drawing surface, ready to receive points.
We loop over each pair using zip, which walks both lists together, giving us one distance d and its matching confidence c each time around.
We turn distance into a column. We scale d across sixty meters onto thirty columns, and min with twenty-nine keeps a big value from falling off the edge.
Now the row. High confidence lands near the top and low near the bottom, using the range one down to point three, again clamped so it stays on the grid.
We drop a lowercase o into the grid at that row and column. That marks where this one detection sits in our little chart.
We set top to one point zero and bot to point three. These are the confidence values at the very top and bottom of our chart, used for labels.
We walk through each row with its index i. Then we compute a confidence label that slides evenly from top down to bottom as we go lower.
We print that label, a divider, then join the row's characters into one string. This draws a full line of the scatter with its confidence marking on the left.
After the rows, we print an axis: a plus and thirty dashes for the bottom line, then a label showing zero meters on the left and sixty meters on the right.
These comments invite you to read your own chart, watching how the o's sink lower as you move right. That downward drift is the story: farther away means less confident.
Finally, two challenges. First, try five-meter buckets and see if the tail is clearer. Second, compute the correlation r and check whether the number matches the picture you drew.
We start with a comment naming this dataset, Anscombe's quartet from 1973. Then we make a list called x123, the x values shared by the first three data sets, so we only type them once.
Here we build a dictionary named sets. Each key is a label like one, two, three, and each value is a pair: the x list and the matching y list. Sets one through three all reuse x123.
Set four is the odd one out, so it gets its own x list where almost every value is eight, with one lonely nineteen, plus its own y values. The closing brace ends the dictionary.
This tiny function, mean, adds up all the numbers in a list and divides by how many there are. That's just the average, and we'll lean on it everywhere.
Now corr computes Pearson's correlation from scratch. First we grab the mean of the x values and the mean of the y values, storing them as mx and my.
We calculate the numerator by pairing each x with its y, subtracting the means, multiplying those differences, and summing them all. This measures how the two move together.
Then dx and dy are the spreads of x and y: we square each difference from the mean, add them up, and take the square root of each total.
Finally we return the numerator divided by dx times dy. That ratio is the correlation, a number telling us how tightly the points hug a straight line.
Let's print results. This line is our header row, labeling the columns for set name, mean of x, mean of y, and r, so the numbers below make sense.
We loop over every set, unpacking each into its name and its x and y lists. Then we print a neatly formatted row showing the two means and the correlation, rounded for readability.
After the loop we print a punchline: statistically these four are quadruplets. The stats come out nearly identical, which is the whole surprise of Anscombe's quartet.
Now we define ascii_plot to actually draw the data. We pick a canvas size of seven rows and twenty-six columns to sketch dots in the terminal.
We build the grid as a list of rows, each row a list of blank spaces. Using a separate list for each row keeps them independent so we can mark points freely.
For each point we pair x with y, then scale the x value into a column and the y value into a row. We flip y because on screen row zero is the top, and clamp so nothing spills off the edge.
With row and column figured out, we drop a little letter o into that spot on the grid, marking where this data point lands.
Then we print the set's name, draw each grid row with a left border bar, and finish with a plus and a line of dashes to form the bottom axis.
Now we loop over the sets again and call ascii_plot for each one, so we can actually see all four scatter plots side by side.
This comment drives home the lesson: same stats, four totally different shapes. Summary numbers are where looking begins, never where it ends.
Finally a challenge for you: find the single point in set three that's bending its line. Remove it, rerun corr, and watch how the r value changes.
